To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
rotavirus vaccines have been shown to be effective in reducing severe rotavirus disease and hospitalizations and that they are safe in developing countries.

(a) rotavirus vaccines are highly efficacious in developed countries and in some developing countries, (b) rotavirus vaccines have been associated with intussusception and other serious adverse events, (c) the risk of intussusception associated with rotavirus vaccine use is low, and (d) there is a need to continue to evaluate rotavirus vaccine safety and efficacy in different populations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the analysis and interpretation of the data obtained from clinical trials of new medical treatments.
the design, synthesis and evaluation of novel materials for use in the development of a new class of drug carriers.
the development and application of new methods and techniques in the fields of theoretical and computational physics and chemistry, in particular with quantum mechanics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both vaccines are safe and effective for global use and that the choice between the two vaccines should depend on the availability of vaccine and cost.
rotavirus vaccines are safe and effective in the developed countries and moderately effective in developing countries.
the two licensed live oral rotaviral vaccines are safe, immunogenic and efficacious in high-income settings and are likely to be safe, immunogenic, and efficacious in most developing countries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vaccine was effective and safe, but not as effective as we had hoped, in low-income countries.

rotavirus vaccines are safe and effective and have been shown to reduce severe rotavirus disease and its complications in high-income and middle income countries of the Americas, Australia, and Europe where they are now being used in routine immunization schedules.
we have a good understanding of the mechanisms of rotavirus infection in the human intestine, and that the virus is able to enter the cell, replicate and exit.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the gradient in immune responsiveness is not due to the genetic makeup of the vaccine strain or its ability to replicate in the gut, but is more likely related to environmental factors such as the nutritional status, hygiene, sanitation, and other factors that may impact the immune response.
the gradient of immune response to the two vaccines is directly related to the socioeconomic status of the population.

the performance of the current vaccines is directly related to the level of socioeconomic development of the country in which the vaccine is administered and the gradient in vaccine efficacy and immune response is directly proportional to the level of development.
